title: Operational SLO Design Lab — Cross-Functional Sprint Brief
content:
Executive summary:

This brief describes the "SLO Design Lab" — a timeboxed, cross-functional sprint to introduce a pragmatic SLO program across Redwood services, validate operational practices with experiments, and produce a lightweight playbook we can adopt company-wide. The approach emphasizes rapid iteration, measurable experiments, and clear operator–product partnership contracts.

Why a Design Lab now:
- Many teams have informal reliability goals; few have measurable SLOs tied to customer outcomes.
- Existing runbooks are inconsistent; we need a repeatable pipeline from SLO definition -> monitoring -> error budget policy -> rollout gate.
- We want to prove lower-friction, low-cost SLOs for common patterns (API latency, inference tail latency, emb-md throughput) before wider rollout.

Goals (outcomes, not activity):
1) Define and publish 3 canonical SLO templates (API request latency, streaming tail latency, and embedding throughput) with measurement definitions and customer-impact justification.
2) Run 2 live experiments: one traffic-shaping shadow canary that exercises fallback behavior tied to an error budget policy; one synthetic fault injection measuring SLO degradation and alert fidelity.
3) Ship a 4-page "SLO Lite Playbook" (templates, metrics, alert thresholds, incident handling, rollout gates) and a simple automation script to create SLO dashboards from a template.
4) Establish a cross-functional intake process that ensures every new public route has an assigned SLO owner and a linked ticket pre-launch.

Scope and constraints:
- Focus only on production-facing HTTP/gRPC inference endpoints and per-route metrics (exclude internal batch/ETL jobs for this lab).
- Use existing observability stack (Prometheus/Tempo/Lightstep/Redwood Console) — no new vendors.
- Work within current capacity: experiments should be safe (no full-scale chaos). Fault injection will be limited to shadow traffic and throttles.

Design Lab cadence (6 weeks):
- Week 0 (Prep): stakeholder kickoff, identify two candidate services (one hosted-api route, one dedicated pool route), collect current metric definitions.
- Week 1–2 (Define & Instrument): finalize SLO definitions, implement metric labels and dashboards, ingest synthetic traffic harness.
- Week 3 (Experiment A — Shadow Canary): run gradual shadow traffic shift to exercise fallback, measure error budget burn and customer-impact proxies.
- Week 4 (Experiment B — Controlled Fault Injection): throttle KV cache / induce slow GPU initialization in staging-like environment while mirroring production read-only traffic for measurement.
- Week 5 (Synthesize & Draft Playbook): write SLO Lite Playbook, produce runbook templates, and automation scripts.
- Week 6 (Review & Handoff): cross-team review, tweak playbook, create follow-up tickets and training sessions.

Roles & responsibilities (practical, not theoretical):
- SRE Lead (Priya Menon): convene lab, own end-to-end experiment safety and final playbook.
- Platform Eng (Marcus Li): dashboard templates, automation script, metric-schema enforcement.
- Product / Hosted API (Asha Nair): customer-impact definition, acceptance criteria for SLO templates, and route owners.
- Serving Runtime (Samantha Ortiz): provide shadow routing hooks, safe fault-injection knobs, and canary fallback code paths.
- Observability Team (Diego Ramos): ensure metric cardinality limits, sampling guidance, and alert rule implementation.
- Solutions Eng & CS (Lina Park): validate playbook against customer commitments and enterprise requirements.

Deliverables (explicit):
- SLO Templates: three markdown templates with measurement query, windowing, numerator/denominator, and rationale.
- Automation: a small CLI (python) that populates a dashboard + alert groups from a template (repo link: github.com/redwood-inference/slo-templates).
- Two experiment reports: shadow-canary-report.md and fault-injection-report.md (each with hypothesis, method, result, decision).
- SLO Lite Playbook (4 pages) and a 30-minute internal training slide deck.

Measurement and success criteria (how we decide):
- Template adoption: at least 4 services (including the two experiment subjects) convert to SLO templates within 8 weeks after lab ends.
- Alert precision: reduce alert-to-incident noise by 25% for instrumented routes during the lab window.
- Error budget policy practical: create a working error-budget gating flow that triggers one automated rollback or traffic shift in an experiment.

Customer impact scoring rubric (used to prioritize routes):
- Public API call with direct user-visible latency: score 10
- Internal API used in critical inference path: score 7
- Non-customer-facing background job: score 1
- Multiply score by QPS weight (1 + log10(QPS)) to prioritize.

Experiment design notes (safety):
- All experiments run first in a shadow mode where traffic is mirrored, not diverted. Shadow canary uses split 0%->10%->50% mirrored traffic and exercises fallbacks in read-only fashion.
- For fault injection, only resource throttles (e.g., limit cache IO, introduce artificial latency via traffic shaping) — no database schema or persistent state changes.
- A pre-flight checklist must be signed off by SRE lead and service owner before any production traffic mirroring begins.

Integration checkpoints (what we'll demo):
- Day 10: live dashboard with SLI queries and demo of metric tagging conventions.
- Day 21: shadow-canary experiment summary and error budget burn visualization.
- Day 33: fault-injection summary and alert fidelity metrics.
- Day 39: Playbook draft and automation tool demo.

Communication plan:
- Weekly sync (30m) with core contributors; public weekly update to #sre-reliability with TL;DR and 1 chart.
- Mid-lab demo open to infra/product leadership at end of Week 3.
- Final playbook and training recorded and posted to Confluence + a short office hours session (1 hour).

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: noisy metrics due to high cardinality. Mitigation: enforce label set and sampling with Platform Eng early in Week 1.
- Risk: experiments accidentally affect customer traffic. Mitigation: shadow-first policy, pre-flight approvals, and a safety kill-switch that disables mirroring within 60s.
- Risk: overwhelmed alerting on experimental noise. Mitigation: route experiment metrics to an experimental alert group that does not page on first run.

Success handoff and long-term plan:
- Within 2 weeks after lab close, create incubation backlog for a 3-month SLO rollout program (templates, lifecycle automation, training).
- Add SLO ownership requirement to new route acceptance checklist in product-ops.
- Plan quarterly SLO health reviews (SLO retros) that synthesize error budget burn trends across product areas.

Appendix: quick checklist for route owners (copy into new-service checklist)
- Has a nominated SLO owner? (Y/N)
- SLO template selected and rationale documented? (Y/N)
- Dashboards created and linked to the route ticket? (Y/N)
- Error budget policy defined (automatic rollback, scale-up, or notify)? (Y/N)
- Pre-flight approved for any shadow or fault-injection experiment? (Y/N)

Next steps (immediate):
- 2026-05-12: Kickoff meeting (Priya to send invite, Marcus to attach metric inventory).
- 2026-05-14: Candidate services confirmed and ticketed (owners assigned).
- 2026-05-17: Platform Eng to produce SLO dashboard template PR.

Open questions (to resolve in Week 0):
- Do we need a lightweight SLO ownership field in our internal service registry? (product-ops input required)
- Can solutions eng sign off on playbook wording regarding enterprise SLAs?
- What is the acceptable minimum observation window for embedding throughput SLOs (30m, 1h, 24h)?

Contact: Priya Menon (pri@redwood-inference.com) — add to Slack #sre-reliability for updates.
